transcript:
This message comes from Angie. Angie has been helping homeowners find skilled pros
to get their home projects done well for over 30 years. For everything from minor repairs
to major remodels, find reviews, pricing, and booking at Angie.com or on the Angie app.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. Democrat Scott Colombe has won the
U.S. Senate race in Mississippi, though the ultimate size of Democrats' majorities in the
House and Senate still remains undetermined one week after Election Day, as more than a dozen
races are still too early to call. Democrats are on track to hold 55 Senate seats in January,
but could pick up one more as votes are counted in Alaska. With at least 255 seats in the House,
Democrats will have their largest majority elected to the chamber since 2008. The Trump
administration is calling for the controversial sale of federal public lands to states, local
governments, and tribes. NPR's Kirk Sigler reports previous attempts to sell off federal land have
drawn bipartisan opposition. On page 24 of the new 28-page U.S. Department of the Interior
Strategic Plan is a brief section that says the agency will "work to decrease the size of the
federal estate by offering to states, localities, and tribes the opportunity to purchase federal
lands." The plan proposes that some of the money from the sales will go back to those entities and
be put toward conserving land. Trump's Interior Department did not immediately respond to a request
for more details, and for now it's unclear how much land would be sold. It's also potentially
legally dubious because Congress has to approve any major federal land sale larger than 2,500 acres.
The plan drew swift criticism from Western environmentalists who said Trump officials want
to turn coveted land used by all Americans over to industry or to states that could never afford
to manage it and would be forced to sell it. Kirk Sigler, NPR News, Boise. The Trump administration
is planning to make it harder to get food aid through the federal government's big grocery
assistance program. It says the proposed rule would close a loophole by no longer allowing some
people who receive benefits from the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program, or TANF,
to automatically be eligible for SNAP, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program,
too. The administration estimates that 6.3 million people could lose eligibility for SNAP.
Russia's Ambassador to the United States has died. The news was confirmed by Russia's
foreign ministry and comes as the Trump administration is seeking to engage Russia
diplomatically over Ukraine and other issues from Moscow. NPR's Charles Maynes has details.
Alexander Darcheev was a student of the Americas, serving as Russia's ambassador
to Canada and other related posts before assuming the role of ambassador to the U.S. last year.
In a post online, the foreign ministry spokesperson said Darcheev died in Moscow due to chronic
disease. In his short tenure in Washington, Darcheev often echoed Kremlin warnings against
the U.S.'s military support for Ukraine and led Russia in negotiations with the Trump
administration aimed at improving ties. He also made fewer headlines than his immediate
predecessors, who had to answer for allegations of Kremlin interference in U.S. elections during
Trump's first term. Darcheev was 66 years old. Charles Maynes, NPR News, Moscow.
U.S. stocks rose today. This is NPR News from Washington.
Millions of Spanish workers have shut down businesses and disrupted transportation in
a protest over housing costs. The strike was the first general strike in Spain in 14 years.
It culminated in tens of thousands of people marching into downtown Barcelona and Madrid.
The protest highlights Spain's housing crisis, with activists demanding government action ahead
of the national election later this month. Democrats say they plan to reverse Medicaid
cuts when they retake control of Congress in January, and Pierre Salina Simmons-Duffin has more.
Medicaid provides health coverage for about 70 million Americans with low incomes.
It's run by states, which have created new IT systems at breakneck speed this past year.
That's because on January 1st, states will have to check whether certain people are meeting new
work requirements or have a medical condition that exempts them. Larry Levitt is with the
nonprofit health research organization KFF. These work requirements start January 1st and
there's enormous uncertainty swirling around them, not just the politics, but
what's going to happen when states turn on the switch and begin implementing this requirement.
Advocates in Nebraska, where the rules have already taken effect,
say the change there has been chaotic and confusing. Salina Simmons-Duffin, NPR News, Washington.
The NBA is seeing an unprecedented number of blowouts this season, with an average winning
margin of 13.8 points per game. That's the most lopsided start in league history.
So far there have been more games decided by 30 points or more than by three points or less.
Chicago is being outscored by 16.7 points per game, which could set a new record. This is NPR.
This message comes from VCU. At Virginia Commonwealth University, research isn't simply
an academic pursuit. It's knowledge put to work. VCU scholars and researchers are expanding what's
known and what's possible across health, science, engineering, the arts, and more. It's the kind of
work that places VCU among the nation's top 50 public research universities. Virginia Commonwealth
University, a world unlike any other. Learn more at vcu.edu.

Trump administration proposes selling federal public lands to states, localities, and tribes via Interior plan

Russian Ambassador to the U.S. Alexander Darcheev dies in Moscow at age 66
Millions of Spanish workers strike over housing costs, first general strike in Spain in 14 years
